input: Learn to whistle with fingers in my mouth

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: There are several distinct finger-whistling techniques (two-handed, one-handed, specific finger combos like index fingers vs. pinkies) — knowing which style they want determines the exact instructions to follow.

Whether they want to use this for a specific situation (hailing a cab, concerts, sports events, general fun) shapes how loud or how reliable the whistle needs to be, and how urgently they need to learn.
How much daily practice time they can commit directly determines how the practice schedule should be structured.
Defining what 'done' looks like — a faint sound, a consistent whistle, or a loud piercing whistle — sets the target and milestone checkpoints.
Knowing if they are self-teaching alone or want a coach/spotter matters for whether the plan includes video resources, a partner giving real-time feedback, or solo drills.
Some learners prefer step-by-step written instructions, video demonstrations, or tactile physical cues — knowing this shapes how guidance should be delivered.
Knowing where they will practice (home, outdoors, shared spaces) affects how they can practice freely without social constraints or noise complaints.

gold.taskDescription: The user wants to learn how to produce a whistle by placing their fingers in their mouth, a physical skill requiring technique, practice, and feedback.

questions.title: Which finger combination do you want to use?
questions.description: Identify the specific finger-whistling technique they want to learn — e.g., two index fingers, two pinkies, one index finger and thumb, etc. This determines the exact physical instructions.

questions.title: What situation do you want to whistle in?
questions.description: Understand the real-world use case — hailing taxis, cheering at events, getting someone's attention at a distance, or just a personal skill — to calibrate how loud and reliable the whistle needs to be.

questions.title: How many minutes a day can you practice?
questions.description: Determine available daily practice time so the plan can be structured realistically — short frequent sessions vs. longer dedicated blocks.

questions.title: What does success look like to you?
questions.description: Clarify the target outcome — any sound at all, a consistent whistle on demand, or a loud piercing whistle — to set clear milestones.

questions.title: Have you ever produced any whistle sound this way?
questions.description: Establish the user's starting point — complete beginner with no sound yet, or someone who occasionally gets a faint noise — to calibrate the difficulty and starting steps of the plan.

questions.title: Do you learn better from videos or written steps?
questions.description: Find out the user's preferred learning format so the plan can point them to video tutorials, detailed written breakdowns, or diagram-style physical cues.

questions.title: Where will you be doing most of your practice?
questions.description: Identify the practice environment — home, outdoors, shared office — to flag any noise or social constraints and suggest appropriate practice times or locations.
